author: Moss, Jessica
title: Akrasia and Perceptual Illusion
ocr_confidence: high (clean text PDF; polytonic Greek in passages renders with some transliteration noise but loci legible)
abstract_paraphrase: DA III.10 presents akrasia as a conflict between phantasia (appearance) and rational cognition: the akratic is torn between an appetite for what appears good to phantasia and a rational wish for what intellect believes good. This makes akrasia parallel to perceptual illusion. Using the de Insomniis on how pathe 'cover over' intellect, Moss reconciles EN VII.3's ignorance account with the struggle account: non-rational desire wins by undermining the cognition that grounds rational desire, not by brute force.

outline.summary: Two puzzles: why a 'Socratic' ignorance account given 'Platonic' struggle resources; how can ignorance be compatible with struggle (Ross's objection). The neglected DA III.10 account.

Section 1. Un-Humean reading of DA III.9-10: action = desire + cognition (intellect OR phantasia); desire is for the good/apparent good; practical cognition is in the first place cognition of things AS good/bad; the present pleasant appears 'good without qualification' just as the sun appears a foot wide; phantasia and doxa are in different parts of the soul (EE VII.2 1235b26-29).

Section 2. Following appearances against knowledge: one cannot act on an appearance actively recognized as false; pathe 'cover over' intellect (de Insomniis), disabling its function of noticing-and-contradicting false appearances; following is 'default yielding,' not active assent (Gallop, Pickave/Whiting); Stoic assent prefigured.

Section 3. Apply to akrasia: temperate person not even subject to the false value-appearance; appetite (bodily pathos) impairs intellect, removing the contradiction, so the agent follows the appearance; pathe can also GENERATE appearances (Rh. II.1 1377b31) - construed as causal chain not vicious circle.

Section 4. EN VII.3 reconciled: 'dry food' syllogism is not akrasia; real account at 1147a10-18 (body-altering pathos; 'has and doesn't have' knowledge); syllogistic/belief-grounded picture (16-17) is one species / difference of emphasis (cf. VII.6 appetite guided by 'logos OR perception'); beasts not akratic (no universal); 'last protasis' = conclusion reading favored; ignorance is literal physical inability; akrasia restricted to strong-passion cases.

Section 5. (1) Because conflict IS perceptual illusion and no one acts on a recognized illusion, akrasia must involve temporary ignorance; (2) the ignorance account is a constitutive PART of the struggle account - appetite wins by knocking out the cognition grounding rational desire.

concepts.label: the illusion account of akrasia
concepts.gloss: Moss's reconstruction: akrasia = conflict between a phantasia value-appearance and rational judgment, structurally identical to perceptual illusion.

concepts.label: value-appearance / appearance of the good
concepts.gloss: phantasia presents things AS good/bad (not merely as cake/predator); a quasi-perceptual, possibly-false evaluative representation.

concepts.label: apparent good (phainomenon agathon) as non-doxastic
concepts.gloss: the object of appetite is what APPEARS good to phantasia, which can be had without (and against) belief that it is good.

concepts.label: un-Humean practical cognition
concepts.gloss: cognition contributes to action not merely by finding means but by finding things good/bad, thereby rendering them objects of desire/aversion.

concepts.label: phantasia vs doxa in different parts of the soul
concepts.gloss: EE VII.2 1235b26-29: the pleasant can appear good to those who do not believe it good; phantasia and belief are distinct faculties.

concepts.label: 'pleasant and good without qualification' (haplos)
concepts.gloss: the value-appearance the non-rational part registers by failing to notice qualifying factors; parallel to 'the sun appears a foot wide.'

concepts.label: noticing-and-contradicting false appearances
concepts.gloss: the defining function of the rational faculty (intellect/doxa); its failure = following phantasia against knowledge.

concepts.label: 'covering over' / 'held in check' of intellect by pathos
concepts.gloss: epikalumma / katechetai: a strong pathos (appetite, emotion, sleep, disease) physically impairs intellect's contradicting-function.

concepts.label: default yielding vs active assent (non-doxastic acceptance)
concepts.gloss: the impaired agent does not positively assent to the appearance; reason 'simply fails to oppose,' so the appearance is accepted by default.

concepts.label: pathos as body-altering and knowledge-impairing
concepts.gloss: appetites/emotions involve bodily changes (DA I.1 403a) that alter cognition, like fever/sleep; the physiologos must explain how the ignorance resolves.

concepts.label: akrasia as temporary, physical, localized ignorance
concepts.gloss: the akratic is literally unable to access the relevant knowledge; not mere failure to combine/use/integrate.

concepts.label: pathe GENERATE false appearances
concepts.gloss: Rh. II.1 1377b31-1378a5: things appear different to the angry/calm, friendly/hostile; a causal-chain (general craving -> distorted appearance -> focused appetite).

concepts.label: beasts not akratic
concepts.gloss: EN VII.3 1147b3-5: animals have only phantasia and memory of particulars, no universal; akrasia requires the rational faculty whose contradicting-function can fail.

concepts.label: Stoic assent (synkatathesis) prefigured
concepts.gloss: the Aristotelian distinction between being-subject-to and rationally-accepting an appearance anticipates the Stoic theory of rational assent to phantasiai.

concepts.label: evaluative phantasia as the seat of character-virtue
concepts.gloss: the virtuous person has CORRECT non-rational value-cognition; character-virtue is the excellent condition of the phantasia-exercising part (n.37).

readings.thesis: DA III.9-10 contains a distinct, neglected account of akrasia as conflict between phantasia and intellect (the 'illusion account').
Practical cognition is in the first place cognition of things AS good/bad (un-Humean); desire follows cognition-of-good.
The apparent good is a quasi-perceptual phantasia-appearance, non-doxastic, that can run contrary to belief.
Akrasia is the practical equivalent of perceptual illusion: appetite follows the value-appearance against rational judgment, as one sees the sun foot-wide against belief.
Non-rational desire wins by UNDERMINING (impairing intellect's contradicting-function), not by brute overpowering; hence akrasia necessarily involves temporary ignorance.
Following-against-knowledge is 'default yielding,' not active assent - NON-DOXASTIC.
EN VII.3's ignorance account is compatible with and supplements the struggle account; 'last protasis' = conclusion reading favored.
Aristotle's akrasia is restricted to cases of strong, body-altering passion (no 'clear-eyed' akrasia).

tensions.desc: EN VII.3 (16-17) grounds appetite in belief/syllogism, but the illusion account grounds it in phantasia; Moss reconciles as 'difference of emphasis' + localized impairment.
Moss's non-doxastic, phantasia-based motivation directly opposes the dissertation's doxa-requirement; the diss's recalcitrance examples are Moss's paradigm cases.
Moss reads de Insomniis 460b3-16 as a WITHIN-EPISODE (synchronic) mechanism, undercutting the dissertation's diachronic-only assignment of the pathetic loop.
'acceptance by default' (Gallop) is more deflationary than the diss's 'involuntary positive taking-as-true'; engages the doxa-gate's conviction-condition.
